name: Nosferatu crypt-lid quick-return
summary: A crank and slotted lever ease a coffin lid open over two-thirds of a turn and slam it in the last third, while a cam on the crank sits the vampire up.

ratio.typical: lid swing 73.7°; open-to-slam time ratio 2.39:1; the occupant rises 72°

topology.notes: ground, crank, slotted lever with the lid, rocker, link and occupant (the hip arm with the figurine on it), with the cam keyed on the crank shaft and the cam roller turning on its stud in the rocker; the crank pin's track roller runs in the lever's slot (pin-in-slot) and the cam roller on the cam (cam contact). The mobility counted from kin is 3: the cam is a body of its own keyed on the crank shaft, and the cam roller's spin on its stud is a passive freedom; the true mobility is 1.

explain.motion: A crank turning steadily about C carries a roller in a slot cut along the lid lever, which pivots at O above it. The lever rocks between two extremes, reached when the crank is square to the slot. Because the crank pin is far from O while it travels the long way round and close to O on the short way, the lever swings slowly one way and fast the other. The lid is fixed to the lever, so it rises 73.7° over 253.7° of crank and falls over 106.3°, a time ratio of 2.39:1. A cam on the crank shaft swings a rocker, and a link carries the swing to the occupant's hip shaft: he sits up 72° while the lid is high, holds, and is lying down again as the slam begins.
explain.forces: Drive torque reaches the lever as a roller force square to the slot, so the lever sees the most force per unit torque on the slam stroke, when the roller is only 20 mm from O. The lid's own weight assists the slam; on the opening stroke the crank lifts it through the long lever arm, so the motor works hardest just after the lid leaves the frame. The cam lifts the occupant with its pressure angle under 22° and lets him down under his own weight.
explain.benefits: One continuously running motor produces the full theatrical sequence: a slow, suspenseful opening, a moment of hesitation at full height, and a fast close. No controller, limit switch or second motor is involved, and the timing never drifts.
explain.limits: There is no true dwell; the lid lingers within 2° of fully open for only 35° of crank, so any occupant must sit up promptly. The slam reverses the roller's load in the slot at speed, which wears the slot flanks first; the Commercial build adds a polymer slot liner rather than relying on the patron's screams to mask the noise.

build.ground: the coffin on its turned legs, the base, the side frame and the hip bracket; the lid hinge O level with the coffin's rim beyond its head end, the crank centre C 50 mm below it, the rocker pivot G and the hip shaft H
build.defining_relations: Lever extremes where the crank is square to the slot: cos β = r/d, β = 53.13° with r = 30 and d = 50. Slam stroke 2β = 106.3° of crank, opening stroke 360° − 2β = 253.7°, time ratio 2.39:1. Lever swing 2 asin(r/d) = 73.74°. Peak lever speed per unit crank speed r/(d − r) = 1.5 on the slam, r/(d + r) = 0.375 on the opening, a factor of 4. Cam, in crank degrees from shut: cycloidal rise from 140° to 212°, dwell to 240°, cycloidal return by 262°. The roller centre stands at the pitch radius rb + s from C (base circle 28 mm, roller 5 mm, lift 12.7 mm) on the arc of the rocker's 32 mm arm about G, so the rocker turns where the two circles meet; the cam's outline is the roller's envelope on that path. The four-bar G, E, F, H (rocker output arm 52 mm at 150° to the roller arm, link 35.4 mm, hip arm 16 mm) turns the swing into 72° at the hip, its transmission angle never under 61°.
build.notes: The input counts from 159° of crank past shut, so the drawing opens with the lid high and the occupant up; the lid and occupant angles read from shut and from lying. Range: crank 360° continuous; lid from 0° (shut) to 73.7° open; occupant from 0° (lying) to 72° (up), fully up from 212° to 240° of crank and lying again by 262°. Lever angle = atan2(−d + r sin θ, r cos θ); lid open = −53.13° − lever angle. The crank turns the way that puts the long arc on the opening. The roller is nearest O at mid-slam, so the slot reaches 14 mm from O. The cam and rocker differ from the first concept's (base 14 mm, lift 18.3 mm, arms 28 and 38 mm): that cam's pressure angle reached 69° on the rise and its outline undercut the roller; a 28 mm base circle and longer arms keep it under 22° with no undercut, and keep the cam's lobe clear of the rocker's axle. The hip shaft stands 106 mm from the hinge, 6 mm further than the concept's, so the occupant's collar clears the open lid by 18.5 mm, not 13. The drive sits close against the drive-side wall on a side frame: the lid hinge's and the rocker's axles stand in it and the crank shaft runs in a housing on its coffin side, with the motor beyond the head end; the hip arm turns on an axle in a small bracket outboard, hung on two standoffs from the side frame, and a tube on it carries the figure through the side frame and the coffin wall.

review.note: T2 review 2026-10-28, six phases drawn from the solved motion at 0, 60, 120, 180, 240 and 300 degrees of crank in VIEW 300 24: tweak. The principle is the crank and slotted lever: the lever's two extremes are the lines from O tangent to the crank circle (the crank square to the slot), drawn as construction lines with the slow opening arc (253.7 degrees) and the quick slam arc (106.3 degrees) of the crank pin between them; the lid tip carries the comet and 15 degree ticks, spread out on the opening and bunched on the slam. The cam, rocker and four-bar that sit the occupant up are second: a detail view of the cam and its roller, and the crown's trace. Changes from the catalogue entry: the cam and rocker were redesigned (base 28 mm, lift 12.7 mm, roller arm 32 mm, output arm 52 mm at 150 degrees, link 35.4 mm, hip arm 16 mm, the hip shaft at 106 mm) because the concept's cam reached a 69 degree pressure angle on the rise and undercut its roller; the timing, the 72 degree rise and the pivots G and H stay. The occupant clears the lid by 18.5 mm (13 in the concept). Default view from the foot end, the drive on the right, so the occupant faces the viewer as he sits up. Solve checks: swing 73.74, time ratio 2.388, rise 72, lingering 35 degrees, pin radius 20 mm, pressure angle 21.2 on the rise.

examples.detail: The standard lid drive for coffins, crypt doors and sarcophagi, where a 20 rpm gearmotor gives a 2.1 s open and a 0.9 s slam, a rhythm scare designers call "the long breath in".
The same quick-return snaps hinged lids on seasonal chocolate boxes, giving the operator time to place the tray on the slow stroke.
Motorised trick-or-treat bowls, where the lid stays near closed for most of the cycle and the quick-return gives children a fair but brief window.
Trapdoor and casket effects, run quietly on the slow stroke and allowed to bang on the fast one because the orchestra covers it.

name: Turkey trot walker
summary: Two Klann legs trot a turkey on a treadmill its own feet drive; the belt works the carving knife and fork behind it, and the turkey gets no further away.

ratio.typical: 94.7 mm stride and 42.5 mm step from a 25 mm crank; the belt runs 188.4 mm back per crank turn

topology.notes: Four groups. The walker: the body on a vertical slide, the crank shaft with its near and far cranks and the cam keyed on it, two Klann legs of four links each, the toes on each ankle pin. The treadmill: two drums and the free belt round them. The fan: the cam roller on a lever pivoted in the body, its rear pin in the spreader's slot, the spreader rising and falling on a guide rod in the rump, and 21 feathers on one pivot, the spreader's rod running in a straight slot in each feather's tail. The cutlery: two cranks on the rear drum, two rods and two carriages on a slide block. The body's height and the belt follow whichever foot is lower, a contact that changes sides at each step: each toe plate is a planar contact on the belt's top face, engaged while its foot is the lower, with the belt moving under it without slip. The mobility counted from kin is not the true one: the far crank and the cam are bodies of their own keyed on the crank shaft, the cam roller's spin on its stud is a passive freedom, and each contact counts only while engaged; the true mobility is 1.

explain.motion: A crank shaft through the turkey's body turns two Klann legs, one on each flank, half a turn apart. Each foot runs back along a low, nearly flat stance of 94.7 mm and lifts 42.5 mm on the way forward. The body hangs on a vertical slide and rests on whichever foot is lower, so it dips up to 4.0 mm at each change of feet: the trot. The foot on the floor pushes a free belt back under the turkey, which therefore walks steadily and goes nowhere. The belt turns the rear roller exactly twice per crank turn, once per step, and two cranks on that roller send the knife and then the fork lunging 24 mm forward on a slide behind the treadmill. A two-lobe cam on the crank shaft spreads the tail fan once every step, from 120° to 165° across its outer feathers.
explain.forces: The body's weight rests on the lower foot and returns through the leg and its two rockers to the crank shaft. The belt is driven only by friction under that foot, so everything behind it, the rollers, the cutlery cranks and the carriages, is driven by the turkey's stride, and their drag comes back through the leg to the crank. At each change of feet the body's vertical motion reverses, a small footfall the slide absorbs.
explain.benefits: One motor works the whole scene. The turkey's walk turns the belt, the belt works the cutlery, and the crank that moves its legs also spreads its fan. No sensor tells the knife where the turkey is, because the turkey is always in the same place.
explain.limits: A Klann foot does not run perfectly flat; two legs half a turn apart leave a 4.0 mm gap at each change of feet, which the sliding body takes up as the trot. The belt moves unevenly, up to 0.82 mm per crank degree, and runs forward 0.54 mm at each change of feet, when both feet are moving forward together; the knife and fork share every surge. The toes are kept level by a spring on the ankle pin, which allows the turkey dignity but not speed.

build.ground: the base, the treadmill frame on turned legs with the drums' shafts in its near rail, the column behind with the body's slide, and the slide block for the cutlery beside the rear drum
build.defining_relations: The leg is a Klann chain retuned for two legs from the library record's proportions (scaled by 1.25 and adjusted): crank 25 mm, A (-22.2, 52.5) and B (-55.4, -17.4) from the crank centre O in the body, CE 55.9, BE 32.7, K (98.4, -6.3) in the frame C to E, HK 77.4, AH 43.8, F (148.4, 42.4) in the frame H to K, E and H closing on the library record's branches. The two legs run half a turn apart, so the lower of the two feet stays within 4.0 mm of the floor; least transmission angle 32°. The body's height is its rest height less the lower foot's height above the lowest point of the foot path, from 0 to 4.0 mm down. The belt moves with the lower foot, 188.4 mm back per crank turn. The drums' radius to the belt's middle is the belt's travel per turn over 4π, 14.99 mm, so the rear drum turns exactly twice per crank turn and the scene repeats every turn. Each carriage is a slider-crank on the rear drum: crank 12 mm, rods 44 and 70 mm, stroke 24 mm, the knife and the fork half a drum turn apart. The fan's cam rises 6 mm twice a turn, by the harmonic law, highest when either foot is at the middle of its stance; the lever turns 4.6° and the spreader moves 7.6 mm, and the spreader's rod runs in a straight slot in each feather's tail, offset from the pivot and laid through the rod's positions at the fan's two extremes, so the outer feathers span 120° closed and 165° spread.
build.notes: Body frame: x forward (the turkey faces +x), y up, z toward the near side; crank angle 0 when the near crank pin C points toward -x, θ increasing counter-clockwise seen from the near side, so the stance foot moves -x. The near foot is lowest at 332.8°, the far foot at 152.8°, and the feet change at 179.5° and 359.5°, where both move forward at 0.10 mm per crank degree, so the support passes without scuffing. The reference pose is the change of feet at 359.5°, both toes on the belt; the cycle opens at 330°. Range: crank 360° continuous, two steps; near foot in the body from x -148.5 to -53.7 and y -71.0 to -28.5; body 0 to 4.0 mm down; belt 188.4 mm per turn; each carriage 24 mm, twice per turn; fan from 120° to 165° across the outer feathers. The toes stand 9 mm under the ankle pin and the belt's top face 9 mm under the lowest point of the foot path. The fan's drive differs from the catalogue entry: the lever's rear pin runs in a slot of the spreader, and the spreader's rod in a straight slot in each feather's tail through the rod's two extreme positions, so the spread is exact at both ends and smooth between.

review.note: T2 review 2026-11-03 on the record, from the solved motion at 330, 30, 90, 150, 210 and 270 degrees of crank: tweak. The principle is the Klann leg and the body riding on whichever foot is lower: the near foot carries the comet with 15 degree ticks, the far foot is traced too, and the change of feet is marked where the body is lowest; the plot gives both feet's heights above the floor with the body's lift, so the bob reads as the lower of the two curves. The belt, the cutlery and the fan are second. Decisions: the reference pose is the change of feet at 359.5 degrees, when both toes are on the belt, and the cycle opens at 330 degrees with the near foot mid-stance and the fan spread; the toes stand 9 mm under the ankle pin; the drums' radius is the belt travel per turn over 4 pi, 14.99 mm. The fan's drive differs from the catalogue entry: the cam roller runs under the cam, its lever lifts a rod along the fan's axis that passes through a straight slot in every feather's tail, each slot offset from the pivot and laid through the rod's positions at the fan's two extremes, because a plate spreader cannot reach the tail pins of 21 feathers stacked on one pivot. Solve checks: stride 94.7 mm, lift 42.5 mm, bob 4.02 mm, belt 188.4 mm per turn, drum two turns per crank turn, carriages 24 mm, fan 120 to 165 degrees, belt speed up to 0.82 mm per degree.

name: Maccabee eight-night indexer
summary: An eight-slot Geneva steps a rack carriage once a night, carrying the shamash along eight fixed candles; each flame flips up as the shamash reaches it.

ratio.typical: 45° of wheel and 20.03 mm of carriage per driver turn; 140.2 mm from the first night to the eighth

topology.notes: ground with the menorah and the back plate, the driver with its locking disc and pin, the Geneva wheel and its pinion keyed on one shaft, the carriage with its rack and lug, the shamash's slider on the menorah's rail, the six pulleys of the steel tape that joins them, and eight flames, each on a hinge at its candle's wick. The pin in the wheel's slots and the locking disc in its arcs alternate; the pinion meshes the rack; the tape's eight runs tie the slider to the carriage through the pulleys; the finger on the shamash's slider meets each flame's lever (a trip contact), and a toggle spring holds each flame up or folded. The mobility counted from kin is not the true one: the pinion is a body of its own keyed on the wheel's shaft, the contacts each count only while engaged, and each flame rests on its toggle spring between trips; the true mobility is 1.

explain.motion: A driver turning once per day carries a pin that enters one of the wheel's eight radial slots, turns the wheel 45° and leaves. For the rest of the turn a locking disc on the driver sits in a concave arc on the wheel and holds it still. A 34-tooth pinion on the wheel shaft drives a rack under the menorah, and a steel tape looped through the menorah's hollow stems and bar makes the shamash, on a slider in front of the row of eight fixed candles, follow the rack's carriage exactly: every index moves it 20.03 mm, one candle to the left. As the shamash arrives, a finger on its slider tips that candle's flame up from where it lies folded back, and a toggle spring holds it up. Night by night the menorah fills from right to left, in keeping with the custom of placing candles from the right.
explain.forces: Load passes from pin to slot flank, and the wheel is accelerated from rest at entry and stopped at exit, with the peak wheel speed at mid-index (0.62 times driver speed for eight slots). At one turn per day these inertial effects are negligible: the carriage averages 0.62 µm/s while indexing, about 130 times the speed of beard growth, which is the comparison clients ask for. The flame's trip takes a few grams at the finger and comes in the last part of the index, when the carriage is slowing. In the dwell the locking arc carries any load on the carriage straight to ground, so pushing the shamash does nothing, by design.
explain.benefits: Exact, repeatable steps with a positive lock between them and no controller, from one motor running continuously. The index is phased away from the evening, so the shamash is always at rest when the candles are lit, and the flames keep the count of the nights without being asked.
explain.limits: Each index occupies 135° of the driver, nine hours at one turn per day, and must be phased to fall between 01:00 and 10:00. After the eighth night the drive is switched off and the carriage returned by lifting the rack out of mesh, a once-a-year operation; a reset tab on the shamash's slider folds the flames down as it passes them on the way back. Candle pitch is fixed at 20.03 mm by the pinion; standard candles fit, but the spacing is not adjustable without changing the pinion, and the Municipal variant uses a 1:12 rack lever to reach street-scale spacing.

build.ground: the base, the carved plinth with the see-through back plate standing on it, the rails under the wheel, and the menorah: two stems, the bar, eight turned cups and their candles
build.defining_relations: r = c sin(π/n) = 22.96 mm and R = c cos(π/n) = 55.43 mm with n = 8 and c = 60 mm; the pin enters each slot radially, so there is no impact along the slot. Index angle 2π/n = 45°; drive angle during index π − 2π/n = 135°, dwell 225°. Carriage step = (2π/n) × m z / 2 = 20.03 mm with z = 34 and m = 1.5 mm. Peak wheel to driver speed ratio r/(c − r) = 0.62. Flame k turns up as the carriage reaches station k: the finger meets its lever in the last 6 mm of the index and tips it past centre, and the toggle spring holds it.
build.notes: Wheel centre W at the origin, driver centre D 60 mm to its right; the rack's pitch line 25.5 mm under the wheel, the carriage on two rails; the cups' tops 92 mm above W, station k at x = 62 − 20.03 (k − 1), night 1 at the right. The stage cycle is eight driver turns, the eight nights, from the first night's evening: the driver's 0 is mid-dwell with the pin pointing away from the wheel, and each index falls in the middle of a turn (112.5° to 247.5°). Seven indexes move the carriage in mesh; the eighth is the yearly return, compressed into the cycle: the rack out of mesh, the carriage carried back 140.2 mm to the first station in step with that index, and a reset tab on the shamash's slider, 10 mm ahead of the shamash, folding flames 8 to 2 as it passes them. The first flame stays up. The shamash stands on a slider on a brass rail under the bar's front, 12 mm above the candles and set forward of the row; a drop on its pan carries the finger and the tab beside the flames. A closed steel tape 2.5 x 0.3 on six pulleys Ø2.4 runs the slider with the carriage: from a lug on the carriage, down behind the wheel into the plinth, round a turnaround at the right, back under the lug to the left stem's foot, up the hollow stem, over a pulley in the bar's left end, along a channel in the bar's foot where the slider's tongue is clamped to it, over a pulley in the bar's right end, down the right stem, round its foot and back over the lug to a turnaround at the left and the lug. The wheel's and the driver's shafts are held by the back plate; the carriage runs on a way and a keeper lip on it. Each flame's lever stands 4.5 mm beside its candle, under the finger's ramp. Range: driver 360° a night; wheel 45° a night; carriage 7 steps, 140.2 mm; flames 0 to 90°, one more each night.

review.note: T2 review 2026-11-05 on the record, from the solved motion at the first night's evening, mid-index, the end of the first index, the fourth night, the eighth night and the yearly return: tweak. The principle is the eight-slot Geneva and the rack it steps: the pin is traced with the comet, the line of centres and the slot line are drawn, and the 135 degree drive window is marked on the pin's circle; the plot gives the carriage's travel against the driver over the eight nights, a staircase of seven steps with long flats, with the flames up as a second line. Decisions: the stage cycle is eight driver turns, the eight nights, opening on the first night's evening with the shamash over the first candle and its flame up. Seven indexes move the carriage in mesh, one station a night to the left, and the finger on the shamash's slider tips each flame over centre in the last 6 mm of its index. The eighth index closes the cycle as the yearly return, compressed into it: the rack is out of mesh, the carriage is carried back 140.2 mm to the first station in step with that index, and a reset tab on the shamash's slider, ahead of the shamash, folds flames 8 to 2 as it passes them going back; the first flame, where the shamash stops, stays up. In the real menorah the drive is off for the return and it is made by hand. The reset is a tab on the slider rather than a separate reset bar under the bar: it needs no motion of its own and folds each flame as the shamash passes it, and it never meets a flame on the way out, since the flames up all lie behind the shamash. A time map slows each index four times, so the step and the trip can be followed, and the yearly return ten times, so the shamash is seen sliding home and folding the flames one by one. The shamash rides the menorah itself, on a slider on a rail under the bar's front, raised above the row and set forward of it; nothing of the drive crosses over the candles. A closed steel tape, as a drafting machine's cable loop, runs it exactly with the carriage, both ways: from the carriage's lug in the plinth round two turnarounds, up the hollow left stem, over a pulley in the bar's end, along the bar's channel past the slider, down the right stem and back. A plain loop would run its top against its bottom; the two turnarounds make the top run go the carriage's way. The tape is mostly hidden (an exception): slots in the stems and along the bar's foot show it. Solve checks: wheel 45 degrees per driver turn, resting 225 degrees; peak wheel speed 0.62 times the driver's; carriage 20.03 mm a night and 140.2 mm from the first night to the eighth; one more flame up each night, 1 to 8.

exceptions.reason: The carriage slides on a way and a keeper lip on the see-through back plate, held into mesh by the pinion, as the catalogue entry's build has it; the slide rule's rails stand on risers from the base, which for a rack in an upright plane would stand in front of the works and through the menorah's stems, so they are not built (polish).

The shamash's slider rides the menorah's own brass rail under the bar's front, its tongue in the bar's channel; the slide rule's rails on risers from the base would stand in front of the menorah, so they are not built (polish).

The steel tape that runs the shamash with the carriage is mostly hidden on purpose, so that nothing of the drive crosses over the candles: it runs inside the hollow stems, the bar's channel and the plinth, where its six pulleys turn; a slot down each stem, the channel's slot along the bar's foot and the pockets at the bar's ends show it and its pulleys. The loop is drawn where it runs, a fixed band that the lug and the slider are clamped to (the belt kit's way).

examples.detail: Municipal variant drives an illuminated shamash along a large outdoor menorah in civic squares, sealed bearings, stainless fasteners, with a lockable hand crank for the annual return.
Community variant on a tabletop menorah, showing at a glance which night it is to anyone who arrives late.
The same eight-station Geneva and rack, run at 60 rpm instead of one turn per day, indexes trays through filling and glazing stations on doughnut lines during the season's peak demand.
Geneva steppers are the traditional drive for film and slide advance; seasonal shop-window displays use this one to advance a scene one panel per day.
